Beyond the Model: Why Data Is Still the Hardest Problem in Enterprise AI
summary:
As frontier models become more widely available, OceanBase is betting on a unified “lakebase” platform and an open-source AI database to win over banks and global enterprises.
 
At fintech conferences over the past two years, one question has dominated conversations about AI: which model is smartest, fastest, or cheapest to use? Banks, insurers, and payment firms have invested heavily in testing frontier models, hoping the right choice might give them a lasting edge.
 
OceanBase CEO Evan Yang believes the bigger challenge lies elsewhere: in the data behind the models.
 
Speaking at OceanBase’s AI Data Conference in Beijing on November 24, 2026, he argued that natural-language tools can make software development look deceptively easy, but the hard work has not disappeared. It has shifted.
 
Drawing on Fred Brooks’s 1986 essay No Silver Bullet, Yang distinguished between “accidental” complexity—the friction better tools can reduce—and “essential” complexity, which remains. In enterprise AI, he said, much of that complexity sits in the data.
 

“The more capable our models become, the more unforgiving our data problems look,” he said. “Solving that essential complexity is the work that will decide who actually captures value from this technology.”
 
Intelligence is becoming more accessible. Proprietary data still matters.
 
As model capabilities spread and prices fall, access to raw intelligence alone may offer less lasting differentiation. For banks and insurers, a more distinctive asset is the data they already hold: transaction histories, risk decisions, operational records, and other information tied to their businesses.
 
In his keynote, Yang highlighted three areas where companies can do more with that data:
 


Private data: Public information is only part of the picture. A company’s own records can provide context that general-purpose models do not have.
Multimodal data: Rows and columns capture only part of reality. Text, images, audio, and sensor feeds can also matter, such as when an insurer assesses an accident or a lender evaluates non-standard collateral.
Well-governed data: Large data volumes are of limited use if they are not indexed, governed, and connected to clear business meaning.
 
OceanLake brings data and AI workloads together
 
To address those gaps, Yang outlined four principles for AI-era data infrastructure: a converged lakebase, multimodal data fusion, governance designed for agents, and openness.
 
At the conference, OceanBase introduced OceanLake, an integrated lakebase AI data platform built around those principles. Unveiled alongside the conference announcement, OceanLake brings transactional, analytical, and AI workloads together on a single copy of data, reducing the need to move information between separate databases, warehouses, and AI stores. The platform also includes a business semantic layer and an agent runtime intended to give AI agents shared context and guardrails.
 
This architectural convergence is notable: Databricks—named a Leader in Gartner’s Magic Quadrant for Cloud Database Management Systems for five consecutive years as of 2025—has made a similar bet with its own Lakebase and LTAP architecture, validating that the durable competitive layer in enterprise AI is the data infrastructure beneath the models.
 
OceanBase cited an early deployment at Ping An Life Insurance, where typical data query delivery times were reportedly reduced from two to five days to about 15 minutes.
 
OceanBase also announced that it is open-sourcing OceanSeek, its agent-focused AI database, under the Apache 2.0 licence. According to the announcement, OceanSeek combines real-time read and write capabilities with analytics, open lake storage, and hybrid search, offering developers an open foundation for agent workloads.
 
Financial-sector credentials and international growth
 
For financial institutions, a new data platform has to meet demanding requirements, especially when it supports payments, ledgers, or regulatory reporting. OceanBase is positioning its AI roadmap on top of a business built in those environments.
 
According to OceanBase’s 2026 conference release, the company achieved revenue compound annual growth of more than 60% over the past five years and generated more than RMB 100 million in AI-related business revenue. Its release also states that it serves 70% of China’s mega-banks with assets above RMB 1 trillion, more than 100 major mid-sized banks, 95% of leading insurers, and 90% of top securities brokers, alongside an estimated share of nearly 30% in China’s financial distributed database market.
 
Internationally, OceanBase’s announcement notes that revenue doubled year over year in 2026, exceeding 15% of total revenue, while its international customer count grew by 300%. Expansion is led by Southeast Asia, with activity also in Japan, the Middle East, and North Africa.
 
Citing an Omdia report released in September 2026 based on 2025 revenue, the announcement notes that OceanBase ranked first among distributed transactional database vendors in Asia and Oceania with a 15.5% share. OceanBase’s release also states that its customer base includes more than 20 leading e-wallets, 50 payment institutions, and 30 fintechs, as well as HSBC, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), and Hang Seng Bank.
 
On the cloud side, OceanBase’s release states that public cloud revenue grew 80% year over year, with multi-cloud accounting for 35% of public cloud revenue and AWS-channel revenue rising 300%.
 
Why data matters in financial services
 
Banks’ AI pilots frequently stall when they encounter fragmented data, inconsistent definitions, or strict access rules across legacy core systems. Those challenges are especially consequential in financial services, where institutions face strict requirements around auditability, regulatory explainability, and continuous uptime.
 
OceanBase’s move into lakebase infrastructure and its decision to open-source OceanSeek reflect its view that enterprise AI will depend on more than capable models and well-crafted prompts. For financial institutions, making data accessible, governed, and meaningful remains a central part of turning AI experiments into dependable services.

Aviva Launches New Lifetime Pet Insurance via Price Comparison Websites
summary:
Aviva today announces the launch of its new Lifetime Pet Insurance product for cats and dogs, helping owners cover the cost of veterinary treatment throughout their pets’ lives.
The new product gives customers greater choice and flexibility when purchasing pet insurance, with a range of annual vet-fee limits, core cover, services such as televet, and optional add-ons, making it easier for them to choose insurance that suits their needs.
The launch forms part of Aviva’s ambition to grow its presence in the UK pet insurance market, building on the insurer’s existing pet insurance offerings available through its Direct Line and Churchill brands.
Flexible lifetime cover
Customers can choose from annual vet fee limits ranging from £1,000 to £12,000, covering treatment for a range of illnesses and injuries, alongside variable excess and co-payment options.
Under the lifetime cover model, if a pet develops an ongoing condition, such as diabetes, after cover has started, customers can continue to claim for treatment year after year, subject to annual limits and provided the policy remains active.
Cover also includes dental treatment following an accident; emergency boarding if a policyholder or family member is unexpectedly hospitalised for more than four consecutive days and is unable to look after their pet; support if a pet is lost or stolen; and cover when travelling with pets in eligible EU countries. Third-party liability protection of up to £2 million is also included for eligible dogs.
Customers also benefit from access to Joii Pet Care, providing unlimited 24/7 chat and video consultations with RCVS*-registered vets via the Joii Pet Care app, as well as personalised treatment plans, symptom checking across 160+ conditions and pet health information.
Aviva Lifetime Pet Insurance will initially be available exclusively through MoneySuperMarket, one of the UK’s leading price comparison websites, before expanding to other major price comparison websites throughout 2027.

Pieter van der Does to Retire as Adyen Co-CEO; Ingo Uytdehaage to Become Sole CEO
summary:
Adyen announces that co-founder and Co-CEO Pieter van der Does will retire effective December 31, 2026. Ingo Uytdehaage, Co-CEO since 2023, will become Adyen’s sole CEO.
Adyen’s 20th anniversary is the right moment to complete the transition. As the company enters its next chapter, Pieter is retiring from his executive role, confident in the direction Adyen has set. He will remain an advisor to Adyen.
Pieter co-founded Adyen in 2006 and led it through its 2018 listing and its growth into a global financial technology platform, averaging double-digit annual growth since 2007. Pieter built Adyen to transform the payments landscape, and has since solved payment complexity for many of the world’s leading businesses. With the acquisitions of Talon.One and Orb, Adyen is extending its ability to deliver differentiated value and win across the full commerce lifecycle, with a strong leadership team in place.
“After 20 years, this is the right moment for me to step down on a positive note and with a very good feeling”, says Pieter van der Does, co-founder and Co-CEO of Adyen. “Adyen has been my life’s work, and I’m incredibly proud of what our teams and customers have built together over the past two decades. Ingo and I have worked very closely together as Co-CEOs, and now we have completed the transition. I have full trust and confidence in Ingo to lead the company into its next exciting chapter.”
“On behalf of the Supervisory Board, I want to thank Pieter for two decades of leadership,” says Herna Verhagen, chair of Adyen’s Supervisory Board. “He built Adyen with conviction, a long-term view and an unusual clarity about what merchants need, and he built it around its people, from a start-up in Amsterdam to a global platform and through its 2018 listing. The company he hands over is ready for its next chapter, and Ingo has the full support of the Supervisory Board as sole CEO. We are glad Pieter will remain available to the company as an advisor.”
“Pieter built more than a company. He built a culture that shapes how we make decisions, how we treat each other and how we put our merchants first, and it will outlast any one of us,” says Ingo Uytdehaage, Co-CEO of Adyen. “I’ve had the privilege of building Adyen alongside him for more than 15 years. I’m grateful for what he has given the company, and our job now is to keep building on what he started. I look forward to executing on the strategy we built together.”
Adyen confirms that there are no changes to standing financial objectives.
